modes: validating: invalid documents graded under onlyValidExecuted (no validate area to tell known errors)
null and absent alike at optional positions
big JSON numbers graded under jsonNumbers

checks.title: Int accepts only integer input values
checks.basis: "When expected as an input type, only integer input values are accepted. All other input values, including strings with numeric content, must raise a request error indicating an incorrect type." What an integer input value is, for JSON, is §3.5's descriptive assertion: numbers "are interpreted as an integer input value if they have an empty fractional part (e.g. 1.0) and otherwise as floating-point input value", which Appendix A counts as a conformance requirement ("descriptive assertions and key words"); the "e.g." is the example, the sentence is not. Accepting an integer input value is CoerceVariableValues' and CoerceArgumentValues' ("If value cannot be coerced ..., raise a request error", otherwise coerce it), algorithm steps Appendix A gives the algorithm's level. October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: Int rejects integers outside the signed 32-bit range
checks.basis: "If the integer input value represents a value less than -2^31 or greater than or equal to 2^31, a request error should be raised." October 2021 says the same. A literal out of range is also not "coercible" (§5.6.1), so an adapter that validates may refuse it at validation: a request error passes there as well as the reference's field error, and only a resolved value fails.

checks.title: Float accepts integer and float input values, and rejects non-finite values
checks.basis: "When expected as an input type, both integer and float input values are accepted. ... All other input values, including strings with numeric content, must raise a request error indicating an incorrect type. If the input value otherwise represents a value not representable by finite IEEE 754 (e.g. NaN, Infinity, or a value outside the available precision), a request error must be raised." October 2021 says the same. A non-finite value such as the literal 1e400 is a MUST failure here; an adapter that validates may refuse that literal at validation (it isn't "coercible", §5.6.1) or at coercion, and only a resolved value fails. A fractional value is kept as its decimal, which the vectors only use with at most 15 significant digits. What "outside the available precision" covers is floatPrecision's.

checks.title: Float and an integer a double can't hold exactly: refused, or rounded to the nearest double
checks.basis: The sentence says a request error "must be raised" for "a value outside the available precision", a term the spec doesn't define. A fraction such as 0.1 has no exact double either, and every implementation rounds it, so the term can't mean every value without an exact double. Coercion.tla's default reading refuses an integer input value a double can't hold exactly (99999999999999999999, 2^53 + 1); its floatRounded switch rounds it to the nearest double, as 0.1 is. Both readings pass, and the report records which happened. It never fails the run. October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: String accepts only string input values
checks.basis: "When expected as an input type, only valid Unicode string input values are accepted. All other input values must raise a request error indicating an incorrect type." October 2021 says the same. A JSON string with a lone surrogate is graded under loneSurrogates, not here, since the spec doesn't define a valid Unicode string.

checks.title: A string literal's escapes and block string indentation decode to its Unicode text
checks.basis: §2.10.4's Static Semantics give a StringValue's Unicode text: each escape sequence's value, and for a block string BlockStringValue(), which removes the common indentation and the leading and trailing blank lines. They have no key word, but they are written as algorithm steps ("Return the Unicode text by ..."), which Appendix A gives the level of the algorithm, they define the value §3.5.3 then accepts, and September 2025 and September 2026 say "Errors encountered during this evaluation ... must result in a parsing error". The vectors use only escapes and block strings whose text is the same in every edition (no braced or surrogate pair escapes). One holds a raw U+1F600, which October 2021's SourceCharacter (U+0009, U+000A, U+000D, U+0020–U+FFFF), read literally as the parse area reads it, leaves out: that vector relies on September 2025's SourceCharacter, any Unicode scalar value (`since`). Expected texts come from Lexer.tla.

checks.title: Descriptions and comments in an executable document don't change the response
checks.basis: §2.2: "Descriptions in GraphQL executable documents are purely for documentation purposes. They MUST NOT affect the execution, validation, or response of a GraphQL document. It is safe to remove all descriptions and comments from executable documents without changing their behavior or results." §6 repeats it in a Note. Each vector is the twin of the same request without the descriptions and comments, and must get the same answer; it rests on that twin (restsOn), so where both fail the same way the failure counts where the twin's does. Descriptions on operations and variable definitions are new in September 2025 (`since`): October 2021's grammar has no Description there, so it can't read those documents. Comments (§2.1.3) are in every edition.

checks.title: Arguments and input object fields in another order mean the same
checks.basis: §2.7: "Arguments may be provided in any syntactic order and maintain identical semantic meaning." §2.10.8: "Input object fields may be provided in any syntactic order and maintain identical semantic meaning." Descriptive assertions, which Appendix A counts as requirements. A JSON variable's map is an unordered map (§3.10), so the order of its keys doesn't matter either. Each vector is the twin of the same request in the written order, and rests on it (restsOn). October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: Boolean accepts only boolean input values
checks.basis: "When expected as an input type, only boolean input values are accepted. All other input values must raise a request error indicating an incorrect type." October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: String and integer input values are coerced to ID strings
checks.basis: "any string (such as \"4\") or integer (such as 4 or -4) input value should be coerced to ID". The format of an ID made from an integer is the service's: any string that writes the integer's exact value passes, such as "1e+21" for 10^21.

checks.title: ID rejects input values other than strings and integers
checks.basis: "Any other input value, including float input values (such as 4.0), must raise a request error indicating an incorrect type." October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: Enums accept their own values, and reject string literals and unknown values
checks.basis: "GraphQL string literals must not be accepted as an enum input and instead raise a request error." For JSON variables, "strings may be interpreted as the enum input value with the same name": a MAY, so taking the string and rejecting it both pass. An unknown value or another kind of input value can't be coerced, so CoerceVariableValues and CoerceArgumentValues raise an error (the vectors also cite §6.1.2 or §6.4.1). October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: Input objects: an object of defined fields, required fields, variables in fields
checks.basis: §3.10: "The value for an input object should be an input object literal or an unordered map supplied by a variable, otherwise a request error must be raised. In either case, the input object literal or unordered map must not contain any entries with names not defined by a field of this input object type, otherwise a request error must be raised." and "If a variable is provided for an input object field, the runtime value of that variable must be used. If the runtime value is null and the field type is non-null, an execution error must be raised." A missing Non-Null field: §3.10 says "If no default value is provided and the input object field's type is non-null, an error should be raised", but §3.12 says "If an argument or input-object field of a Non-Null type is not provided, is provided with the literal value null, or is provided with a variable that was either not provided a value at runtime, or was provided the value null, then a request error must be raised." Both are normative prose about the same case; §3.12's is the stronger and more specific requirement, and accepting such a value would break it, so the check is a MUST and those vectors cite §3.12. Field defaults are a "should", graded by inputFieldDefaults. October 2021 says the same ("a field error must be raised" for the null variable).

checks.title: An omitted input field gets its default value
checks.basis: "If no value is provided for a defined input object field and that field definition provides a default value, the result of coercing the default value ... should be used." The SHOULD applies to each field: a result that is right except that it leaves out some or all of such defaults fails this check, not inputObject.

checks.title: OneOf input objects take exactly one non-null field
checks.basis: §3.10.1, new in September 2025 (October 2021 has no OneOf Input Objects): the value "must contain exactly one entry and that entry must not be null or the null literal, otherwise a request error must be raised", and "The resulting coerced map must contain exactly one entry and the value for that entry must not be null, otherwise an execution error must be raised." The vectors are §3.10.1's table of examples and a few more, on a schema of their own (the vectors' `schema: "oneOf"`), all `since` September 2025. September 2026 says the same.

checks.title: Lists: each item coerced, a single value wrapped in a list
checks.basis: An item that isn't a list, where the item type is a list, is coerced as a list of one: "list values are accepted only when each item in the list can be accepted by the list's item type", and a value that is "not a list" is accepted by a list type as "a list of size one". That prose is the same in every edition. October 2021's table of examples says "Error: Incorrect item value" for [1, 2, 3] as [[Int]], but examples are non-normative ("Examples in this document are non-normative"), and the tables of September 2025 and September 2026 give [[1], [2], [3]]. So these vectors carry no `since`, and the table's answer fails this check under a finding of its own. A list item that is a variable whose runtime value isn't a list, where the item type is a list ([$x, [$x]] for [[Int]] with $x: Int), is only in an invalid document (§5.8.5), and the spec doesn't say whether the value is used as it is (§6.4.1's Note: variable values are already coerced) or wrapped as "a list of size one": both pass, for adapters that execute invalid documents.

checks.title: Non-Null rejects null
checks.basis: "If an argument or input-object field of a Non-Null type is not provided, is provided with the literal value null, or is provided with a variable that was either not provided a value at runtime, or was provided the value null, then a request error must be raised." October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: CoerceVariableValues: defaults, missing and null values, and failures as request errors
checks.basis: The algorithm's steps: a missing variable with a default gets "the result of coercing defaultValue"; "Otherwise if variableType is a Non-Nullable type, and either hasValue is not true or value is null, raise a request error"; a null value is kept; "If value cannot be coerced according to the input coercion rules of variableType, raise a request error." Algorithm steps have the algorithm's level (Appendix A). September 2025 says the same. October 2021 adds the default as it is (see the vectors `since` September 2025) and otherwise says the same.

checks.title: CoerceArgumentValues: defaults, missing variables, and null for Non-Null arguments
checks.basis: The algorithm's steps: an argument with no value, or whose variable has no runtime value, gets "the result of coercing defaultValue" if it has one; an explicit null is kept; a variable's value is used as it is; a literal is coerced; "Otherwise if argumentType is a Non-Nullable type, and either hasValue is not true or value is null, raise an execution error." Algorithm steps have the algorithm's level (Appendix A). Whether a failure is an execution error or a request error is argumentErrorKind's. September 2025 says the same. October 2021 adds the default as it is (see the vectors `since` September 2025) and otherwise says the same.

checks.title: A value CoerceArgumentValues can't coerce is a field error, not a request error
checks.basis: The input coercion rules call the failure a request error (§3.5: "If an input value does not match a coercion rule, a request error must be raised"; §3.12: "... then a request error must be raised"). CoerceArgumentValues says "raise an execution error", and September 2026 settles the conflict with a SHOULD (September 2025 has the same sentence): "Any request error raised as a result of input coercion during CoerceArgumentValues() should be treated instead as an execution error." So a request error where the reference gives a field error fails only this SHOULD. Except where §3.10 or §3.10.1 itself says "an execution error must be raised" (a variable in an input object literal whose runtime value is null at a Non-Null field; a OneOf literal whose one entry is a variable with a null or no runtime value): those vectors (`executionErrorRequired`) fail their own check. October 2021's CoerceArgumentValues says "raise a field error" and has no such sentence, while its §3.5 and §3.12 still say a request error must be raised; the kit takes the weaker reading there too, the same SHOULD.

checks.title: An argument error below the root nulls the field's position and propagates
checks.basis: For the vectors with fields below the root (capability nested-fields). CoerceArgumentValues raises an execution error, and §6.4.4: "If an execution error is raised while resolving a field (either directly or nested inside any lists), it is handled as though the response position at which the error occurred resolved to null, and the error must be added to the errors list"; "Since Non-Null response positions cannot be null, execution errors are propagated to be handled by the parent response position"; "If a List type wraps a Non-Null type, and one of the response position elements of that list resolves to null, then the entire list response position must resolve to null." So the data must show null at the field's position, or at its nearest nullable parent's, one error per position (each item of a list is one), and no call of the field's resolver. Where every position up to the root is Non-Null, "the data entry in the execution result should be null": the reference gives null there, and no other data can be right. The error's path is fieldErrorPath's (§7.1.6), including list indices and aliases (§7.1.4: "If a path segment is associated with an aliased field it must use the aliased name"). A value below the root is graded the same way: one call at each position, with the coerced arguments. October 2021 says the same with "field error".

checks.title: CreateSourceEventStream: the source stream's resolver gets the field's coerced arguments
checks.basis: For the subscription vectors (capability subscription-source). CreateSourceEventStream: "Let fieldName be the name of the first entry in fields. Note: This value is unaffected if an alias is used.", "Let argumentValues be the result of CoerceArgumentValues(subscriptionType, field, variableValues)", and ResolveFieldEventStream: "Return the result of calling resolver, providing rootValue and argumentValues." Then each event executes the root selection set (§6.2.3.2), so the response stream's first result holds the field under its response name, and the field's resolver gets the same coerced arguments. Algorithm steps have the algorithm's level (Appendix A). October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: An error while establishing a subscription's source stream is a request error
checks.basis: New in September 2026. §6.2: "Operation execution begins when the execution algorithm for the operation type is invoked: ExecuteQuery() for query operations, ExecuteMutation() for mutation operations, and Subscribe() for subscription operations." ExecuteRequest runs CreateSourceEventStream before Subscribe, and §7.1.5: "If an error was raised before operation execution begins, the response must be a request error result which will result in no response data." §7.1.6 lists among request errors a "failure to establish a source event stream for a subscription operation", and §6.2.3.1's Note says "an error raised here will be a request error". The vectors have the source stream's resolver raise (`subscribe: "raise"`). September 2025 runs CreateSourceEventStream inside Subscribe and doesn't list it, so these vectors have `since` September 2026.

checks.title: A subscription root field's argument that can't be coerced is a request error
checks.basis: §6.2: "Operation execution begins when the execution algorithm for the operation type is invoked: ExecuteQuery() for query operations, ExecuteMutation() for mutation operations, and Subscribe() for subscription operations." ExecuteRequest runs CreateSourceEventStream before Subscribe, and CreateSourceEventStream: "Let argumentValues be the result of CoerceArgumentValues(subscriptionType, field, variableValues)." §7.1.5: "If an error was raised before operation execution begins, the response must be a request error result which will result in no response data." So an argument of the subscription root field that can't be coerced must give a request error result. CoerceArgumentValues calls the error it raises an execution error, and §6.4.1 says "Any request error raised as a result of input coercion during CoerceArgumentValues() should be treated instead as an execution error"; those name the error, while §7.1.5 says what the response must be when it is raised before operation execution, and §6.2.3.1's Note agrees: "The call to CreateSourceEventStream() occurs before operation execution begins, and thus an error raised here will be a request error." An execution error (a result with data) fails here, and accepting the value fails the type's own check (`nonNull`, `int`). September 2025 runs CreateSourceEventStream inside Subscribe, after operation execution begins, so these vectors have `since` September 2026.

checks.title: Selections only an invalid document has: a missing fragment and an undefined field are skipped, a second subscription root field is a request error
checks.basis: For adapters with `unvalidated` (others get these as invalid documents, under invalidNotExecuted or onlyValidExecuted). CollectFields: "If no such fragment exists, continue with the next selection in selectionSet." ExecuteCollectedFields: "Let fieldType be the return type defined for the field fieldName of objectType. If fieldType is defined: ...", so a field the type doesn't define has no entry in the result. CreateSourceEventStream: "If collectedFieldsMap does not have exactly one entry, raise a request error." CollectFields collects every field selection, defined or not. Algorithm steps have the algorithm's level (Appendix A). October 2021 has the same steps.

checks.title: GetOperation: the operation operationName names, or the only one, else a request error
checks.basis: GetOperation: "If operationName is null: If document contains exactly one operation. Return the Operation contained in the document. Otherwise raise a request error requiring operationName." and "Let operation be the Operation named operationName in document. If operation was not found, raise a request error." Includes a mutation running on the mutation root type, and only the selected operation's variables being coerced. Algorithm steps have the algorithm's level (Appendix A). October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: A document with a type system definition isn't executed
checks.basis: §2.3: "Documents are only executable by a GraphQL service if they are ExecutableDocument and contain at least one OperationDefinition. A Document which contains TypeSystemDefinitionOrExtension must not be executed; GraphQL execution services which receive a Document containing these should return a descriptive error." and "GraphQL services which only seek to execute GraphQL requests and not construct a new GraphQL schema may choose to only permit ExecutableDocument." So the answer is a request error, whether the service refuses the document at parsing, at validation (§5.1.1 Executable Definitions) or before executing it, and even where it also holds an operation that would run. Graded under this check for every adapter, validating or not: the sentence doesn't depend on validation. October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: A document that doesn't parse is a request error
checks.basis: §6.1: "To execute a request, the executor must have a parsed Document". §7.1.6: "Typically raised before operation execution begins, a request error may occur due to a parse grammar or validation error in the Document", and "If a request error is raised, the response must be a request error result. The data entry in this map must not be present, the errors entry must include the error, and request execution should be halted." Parser.tla says which documents don't parse. Graded for every adapter, validating or not: no answer but a request error passes. October 2021 says the same (§7.1.2: a request error "is raised before execution begins", and the data entry "must not be present").

checks.title: A document with known validation errors fails as a request error, without executing
checks.basis: "If validation errors are known, they should be reported in the list of \"errors\" in the response and the request must fail without operation execution." The MUST holds only where the errors are known: graded for adapters without `unvalidated` that claim `validate`, on vectors Validation.tla rejects and the implementation's own validator (asked through the validate area) rejects too. A request error, no data, no resolver called. October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: Only valid documents are executed
checks.basis: "only operations from documents which pass all validation rules should be executed" (§6.1.1), and "execution should only occur for valid requests" (§5). Graded for adapters without `unvalidated`, on vectors Validation.tla rejects whose errors the implementation's validator doesn't report (it accepts the document in the validate area, or the adapter doesn't claim validate, so the kit can't tell). Such a document is a validation rule the implementation misses, which the validate area grades at MUST; executing it is only this SHOULD. October 2021 says the same.

checks.title: A valid document isn't rejected at validation
checks.basis: As the validate area's check of the same name: a document that breaks no validation rule is valid, and must not be refused as invalid. Graded for adapters without `unvalidated` that claim `validate`: a valid vector answered with a request error whose document the implementation's own validator rejects (asked through the validate area) fails here, not under the coercion rule the vector is about, whether or not the reference's answer is also a request error.

checks.title: A request error result has no data entry
checks.basis: September 2026 and September 2025, §7.1.3: "The request error result map must not contain an entry with key {"data"}." October 2021, §7.1: "If the request failed before execution, due to a syntax error, missing information, or validation error, this entry must not be present." and §7.1.2: "If a request error is raised, execution does not begin and the data entry in the response must not be present." Its §7.1.1 also says "should not be present", but the two MUST sentences are the ones about request errors, so the check is a MUST in every edition. A request error with "data": null is still a request error for the vector's own check, and fails this one.

checks.title: A request gets a response
checks.basis: "When a GraphQL service receives a request, it must return a well-formed response." October 2021 says the same. The adapter answers with an `error` when the implementation produced no response at all, for example because it threw. Execution's check of the same name grades the same sentence. No response says nothing about the coercion rule the vector is about, so it always counts here, whatever the reference's answer; the finding names that rule as a hint. Every vector exercises this check.

checks.title: A field error's path is the field's response path
checks.basis: §7.1.6: an error that "can be associated to a particular field in the GraphQL result ... must contain an entry with the key {"path"} with a response path which describes the response position which raised the error". §7.1.4: a response path names response positions, not arguments. A result whose data holds the field as null, with one error and no resolver call, is a field error whatever its path. If that is the answer the vector expects, a path other than the field's fails this check. Every vector that accepts a field error exercises it. October 2021's §7.1.2 keeps the must: the error "must contain an entry with the key path that details the path of the response field which experienced the error". Its shoulds there are about the path's form ("should be a list of path segments", indices "should be 0-indexed integers"), not about which field it names, so a path to the argument (`["v"]`) fails a MUST in every edition. September 2025 and September 2026 have the same §7.1.6 sentence.

checks.title: Every error is a map with a string message
checks.basis: "Every error must contain an entry with the key {"message"} with a string description of the error", and each error "must be a map" (§7.1.1, §7.1.3). October 2021 says the same ("each error is a map", "Every error must contain an entry with the key message"). A result whose errors aren't all maps with a string message, such as [null], or a field error with only a path, fails this check wherever its outcome would otherwise match. Every vector exercises it.

checks.title: errors, when present, is a non-empty list
checks.basis: The same check as execution's. September 2026, §7.1.1: "If any errors are raised during operation execution, the execution result must contain an entry with key {"errors"}. The value of this entry must be a non-empty list ... If the request completed without raising any errors, this entry must not be present." October 2021, §7.1: "If the request raised any errors, the response map must contain an entry with key errors. ... If the request completed without raising any errors, this entry must not be present." Its §7.1.2 also says "should not be present", but the §7.1 MUST is the sentence about the entry, so the check is a MUST in every edition, as in execution. September 2025 says the same ("If execution raised any errors ..."). A value with "errors": [] is still a value for the vector's own check, and fails this one. Every vector exercises it.

checks.title: The response is a map
checks.basis: §7.1.1: "An execution result must be a map." §7.1.3: "A request error result must be a map." A result whose `response` is a list, a string, a number, a boolean or null fails here, rather than being taken as an adapter that doesn't follow the result format. Execution's check of the same name. October 2021, §7.1: "A response to a GraphQL request must be a map." Every vector exercises it.

checks.title: The result has no entries besides data, errors and extensions
checks.basis: "To ensure future changes to the protocol do not break existing services and clients, the execution result and request error result maps must not contain any entries other than those described above." October 2021, §7.1: "the top level response map must not contain any entries other than the three described above". The same check as execution's, applied to every result here, request errors included. A result with another top-level entry is still classified, and fails this check wherever its outcome would otherwise pass. Every vector exercises it.

checks.title: extensions, when present, is a map
checks.basis: "The \"extensions\" entry in an execution result or request error result, if set, must have a map as its value." October 2021, §7.1: "This entry, if set, must have a map as its value." The same check as execution's. A result whose top-level extensions isn't a map is still classified, and fails this check wherever its outcome would otherwise pass. Every vector exercises it.

checks.title: JSON strings with a lone surrogate: kept as sent, replaced with U+FFFD, or refused
checks.basis: §3.5.3 accepts "only valid Unicode string input values" without defining one, and calls a String "a sequence of Unicode code points", which a lone surrogate is. §3.5.5 says nothing about Unicode. RFC 8259 §8.2 calls the behaviour of software that receives such a string unpredictable. Coercion.tla refuses it, but the check also passes the value kept as sent and the value with U+FFFD, and records which happened. It never fails the run.

checks.title: JSON numbers a double can't hold: read exactly, read as binary64, or refused
checks.basis: Not a GraphQL rule: RFC 8259 §6 lets a JSON parser limit the range and precision of numbers. Vectors whose answer depends on that count here, never against Float or ID, unless the adapter claims exact-numbers.

checks.title: A request's extensions with keys of no meaning to the service leave the response as it is
checks.basis: §6: a request's "extensions (optional): A map reserved for implementation-specific additional information." and "If present, extensions must be a map, but there are no additional restrictions on its contents." The spec gives the entries no meaning and lets an implementation give them one, so it doesn't require a service to ignore them. The vectors (capability request-extensions) send keys under a prefix no service uses, each the twin of the same request without extensions, and record whether the answer stays the same. It never fails the run. October 2021 has no request extensions.
checks.note: the same answer as without extensions: 3
